title: What are @QueryHints in JPA, what hints like readOnly, cacheable, fetchSize, and timeout control, and how do method-level and transaction-level settings differ?

s1_definition.profdef: `@QueryHints` attaches JPA/Hibernate query hints to a repository method to tune a specific query's execution. Common hints include `org.hibernate.readOnly` (load entities read-only, skipping dirty-check snapshots), `org.hibernate.cacheable` (use the query cache), `org.hibernate.fetchSize` (JDBC fetch size for streaming large results), and `jakarta.persistence.query.timeout` (abort a query after N milliseconds). Method-level hints apply to one query, whereas transaction-level settings like `@Transactional(readOnly=true)` apply to the whole transaction.
s1_definition.analogy: Query hints are special instructions National Bank of India pins to a single request slip. "readOnly" tells the clerk "I'm only reading, don't bother snapshotting for changes." "cacheable" says "if you fetched this exact list recently, reuse it." "fetchSize" says "bring records to me in bundles of this many instead of all at once or one by one." "timeout" says "if this takes longer than three seconds, give up." Pinning the note to one slip (method level) affects just that request; posting it on the department door (transaction level) affects everything that happens during the whole visit.
s1_definition.oneliner: @QueryHints fine-tune a single query (readOnly, cacheable, fetchSize, timeout); @Transactional(readOnly) sets the policy for the whole transaction.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `@QueryHints` attaches JPA/Hibernate query hints to a repository method to tune a specific query's execution. Common hints include `org.hibernate.readOnly` (load entities read-only, skipping dirty-check snapshots), `org.hibernate.cacheable` (use the query cache), `org.hibernate.fetchSize` (JDBC fetch size for streaming large results), and `jakarta.persistence.query.timeout` (abort a query after N milliseconds). Method-level hints apply to one query, whereas transaction-level settings like `@Transactional(readOnly=true)` apply to the whole transaction.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Query hints are special instructions National Bank of India pins to a single request slip. "readOnly" tells the clerk "I'm only reading, don't bother snapshotting for changes." "cacheable" says "if you fetched this exact list recently, reuse it." "fetchSize" says "bring records to me in bundles of this many instead of all at once or one by one." "timeout" says "if this takes longer than three seconds, give up." Pinning the note to one slip (method level) affects just that request; posting it on the department door (transaction level) affects everything that happens during the whole visit.

**One line to remember:** @QueryHints fine-tune a single query (readOnly, cacheable, fetchSize, timeout); @Transactional(readOnly) sets the policy for the whole transaction.

sections.s2_technical:
`@QueryHints(@QueryHint(name = "org.hibernate.readOnly", value = "true"))` on a method loads the returned entities in read-only mode, so Hibernate does not take a dirty-check snapshot and will not flush changes for them. This saves memory and CPU on large read queries even within a writable transaction, and it is more granular than marking the whole transaction read-only.

`org.hibernate.cacheable = true` makes the query use Hibernate's query cache (which must be enabled). For a frequently repeated, rarely changing query like a list of branch codes, the result is cached and reused, avoiding repeated database hits. You pair it with a second-level cache region.

`org.hibernate.fetchSize` sets the JDBC fetch size, controlling how many rows the driver pulls per round trip. For streaming a huge export, a fetch size like 1,000 prevents loading everything into memory at once; combined with a Stream return type and read-only, it enables memory-safe processing of millions of rows.

`jakarta.persistence.query.timeout` (milliseconds) aborts a query that runs too long, protecting the system from a runaway report locking resources. There is also `jakarta.persistence.lock.timeout` for how long to wait for a pessimistic lock.

Method level versus transaction level: a method-level hint affects exactly that query. Transaction-level readOnly affects every query in the transaction, sets the connection read-only, and changes the flush mode. They compose: you might have a writable transaction but mark one heavy reporting query read-only via a hint. The timeout hint on a method bounds that query; a transaction timeout (@Transactional(timeout=...)) bounds the whole transaction.

Senior nuances: the query cache only helps if the underlying entities are also cached and the data is read-mostly; otherwise it adds overhead and invalidation churn. fetchSize behaviour is driver-specific (PostgreSQL needs autocommit off to honour it). readOnly at the method level is a great default for list endpoints because it halves the memory of loaded entities. Always set a query timeout on customer-facing endpoints so a slow query degrades gracefully rather than exhausting the connection pool.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A list endpoint returns thousands of accounts for display only. Tracking them for changes wastes memory. This is exactly the method-level readOnly hint.

Problem 2 — A query for the fixed list of branch codes runs constantly and the data almost never changes. This is exactly the cacheable hint.

Problem 3 — A regulatory export streams millions of transactions and must not load them all into memory. This is exactly the fetchSize hint with streaming.

Problem 4 — A customer-facing search must never hang the thread pool on a slow query. This is exactly the query timeout hint.

We will build a repository whose methods carry the appropriate hints and a service that uses them.

# Run
java -jar target/query-hints-service-1.0.0.jar

# Read-only list

curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts/branches

sections.s5_journey:
Input: list ACTIVE accounts; fetch branch codes twice; stream all; search by name.

Step 1 — activeList calls listReadOnly carrying the readOnly hint. Hibernate loads the accounts without taking dirty-check snapshots, so they occupy roughly half the memory and will never be flushed as updates. This happens even though the method could be in a writable transaction.

Step 2 — branches calls branchCodesCached with the cacheable hint. The first call runs the SQL and stores the result list in the query cache. The second call within the cache window returns the cached list without touching the database, saving a round trip for this constant, rarely-changing data.

Step 3 — exportCount calls streamAll with fetchSize 1000 and readOnly. The JDBC driver pulls 1,000 rows per round trip instead of materializing millions at once, so memory stays flat while the stream is consumed inside the transaction, then the stream is closed.

Step 4 — search calls searchByName with a 3,000-millisecond timeout hint. If a wildcard search scans too long, the database aborts it and Hibernate throws a QueryTimeoutException rather than tying up the thread and a pooled connection indefinitely.

```
Hibernate: select ... where status=?            (readOnly: no snapshot)
Hibernate: select distinct branch_code ...       (cacheable: first call only)
INFO  branches second call served from query cache (no SQL)
Hibernate: select ... (fetchSize 1000, streamed)
INFO  Streamed 2 accounts for export
Hibernate: select ... where holder_name like ?   (timeout 3000ms)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```

    │
    ├─ readOnly hint   → load without dirty-check snapshot (half memory)
    ├─ cacheable hint  → 1st call SQL, 2nd call query cache (no DB)
    ├─ fetchSize 1000  → stream rows in bundles (flat memory)
    │    + readOnly, consumed inside txn, stream closed
    └─ timeout 3000ms  → abort slow search → QueryTimeoutException
    ▼
  Fast, memory-safe, resilient reads

  Method-level hint → one query
  @Transactional(readOnly) → whole transaction policy
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Query hints let me tune an individual query's execution without changing what it returns. I attach them with the QueryHints annotation on a repository method. The readOnly hint tells Hibernate to load the returned entities without taking a dirty-check snapshot, which roughly halves their memory footprint and guarantees they are never flushed as updates; this is more granular than a read-only transaction because I can apply it to one heavy query even inside a writable transaction. The cacheable hint routes a query through Hibernate's query cache, which is ideal for constant, rarely-changing lookups like branch codes that are read over and over. The fetchSize hint controls how many rows the JDBC driver pulls per round trip, which is essential for streaming huge result sets so memory stays flat rather than materializing millions of rows at once. The query-timeout hint aborts a query that runs too long, protecting the system from a runaway report.

The method-level versus transaction-level distinction matters. A query hint affects exactly one query, while a transaction-level setting like read-only or timeout on the Transactional annotation applies to every query in the transaction, and read-only additionally sets the connection read-only and changes the flush mode. They compose cleanly: I can run a writable transaction overall yet mark one expensive reporting query read-only through a hint, and I can bound a single query with a query timeout while bounding the whole transaction with a transaction timeout.

In our National Bank of India system, list endpoints that only display data use the method-level readOnly hint to save memory, the branch-code lookup uses the cacheable hint because it is read constantly and almost never changes, the regulatory export streams millions of transactions with a fetch size of a thousand plus read-only so it never blows up the heap, and every customer-facing search carries a three-second query timeout so a slow wildcard search degrades gracefully instead of exhausting the connection pool.

The senior cautions I give are that the query cache only pays off when the underlying entities are also cached and the data is genuinely read-mostly, otherwise invalidation churn makes it a net loss; that fetch size behaviour is driver-specific and PostgreSQL in particular needs autocommit off to honour it, which is why I keep streaming inside a transaction and close the stream; and that setting a query timeout on customer-facing endpoints is not optional in banking, because one slow query without a timeout can cascade into a pool exhaustion outage.
